items.scenario: A teammate shares a blog post claiming a new Claude Code setting changes how permission rules are evaluated, and wants to update the team's shared settings today.
items.question: Where do you confirm the behaviour before changing anything?
options: The official Claude Code documentation and its changelog for that release
The claude.ai app help centre, since it documents every Claude product
Ask Claude Code to describe the setting's behaviour and trust its answer
The blog post's own examples, run once against the team's main branch
items.explanation: Each surface has its own authoritative docs: Claude Code's documentation and release notes for Claude Code, the help centre for the apps, the platform docs for the API. A third-party post, or the model's own description, is not evidence of current behaviour.
distractors: Wrong surface: the app help centre covers claude.ai, desktop and mobile, not Claude Code configuration.
The model may not know a setting newer than its training data and can describe it confidently and wrongly.
One run against main tests nothing reliably and risks the shared branch on an unverified claim.

items.scenario: An agentic session ran overnight as a scheduled task to file 200 scanned invoices into folders and rename them. This morning its summary says 'All invoices filed successfully.'
items.question: What should your review focus on?
options: The summary message, since it reports the overall outcome of the run
The actions it took: which files moved, were renamed or were removed
Whether it finished inside the usage window, as a sign it worked well
Nothing yet; scheduled tasks are reviewed by admins in the audit log
items.explanation: In chat you check an answer; in an agentic session you check actions. A summary can omit or misdescribe what was done, so verify the moves, renames and any deletions themselves.
distractors: A summary is the model's description of its work, not evidence of it.
Finishing quickly says nothing about whether files went to the right place.
Audit logs support investigation after the fact; they don't replace your own review of the run.

items.scenario: For the next quarter you'll repeatedly ask questions about the same 15 architecture documents and your team's decision log.
items.question: Which surface fits best?
options: A new chat each time, re-uploading whichever documents seem relevant
A Project holding the documents, with instructions on how to answer
Claude Code, pointed at a folder where the documents are saved locally
A small internal tool on the API that loads the documents per question
items.explanation: 'Work on my documents' that recurs maps to a Project: the files and instructions persist, so every chat starts with the same context.
distractors: Re-uploading is repetitive, and each chat sees a different subset, so answers drift.
Claude Code is for working in a code repository, not for Q&A over a document set.
The API is for building product features; it's overkill for one team's reading.

items.scenario: Your team co-edits a Google Doc design proposal with comment threads. You want Claude to tighten section 3 without losing the comments or the edit history.
items.question: What is the best route?
options: Copy section 3 into a chat, get a rewrite, and paste it back over the original
Use the Docs live-editing connector so the edit happens inside the document
Export the Doc as a PDF, upload it to a chat, and retype the suggested edits
Download it as .docx, edit it in a chat, and upload the result as a new file
items.explanation: Work inside an Office or Google file belongs in the add-in or connector for that file, so the edit lands in place and the team's comments and history stay intact.
distractors: Pasting over the text can orphan comment threads and bypasses the document's own review flow.
Adds manual retyping, a lossy format and a chance to introduce errors.
Creates a second version that diverges from the one the team is commenting on.

items.scenario: You need realistic data to reproduce a bug in a user-import pipeline that fails on unusual names and duplicate IDs.
items.question: What should you give Claude?
options: A sample of 50 real rows from the production users table, as exported
The schema and the edge cases, asking it to generate synthetic records
The production rows with surnames removed and emails left in place
Nothing; bugs that involve user data can't be worked on with an AI tool
items.explanation: Synthetic stand-ins keep the shape and edge cases without personal data. That's minimisation in practice.
distractors: Production personal data is on the never-paste list.
Partial removal still leaves identifiable personal data (first names, emails, IDs).
Over-correction. Synthetic data makes this safe.

items.scenario: Your manager asks you to draft talking points about an unannounced reorganisation, on your company seat. You don't want the details resurfacing later in unrelated chats.
items.question: Which approach fits?
options: A normal chat, then ask Claude at the end to forget what it was told
An incognito chat, knowing org retention and admin settings still apply
A team Project, so the draft sits with the other team documents
Your personal account, so nothing touches the company workspace
items.explanation: Incognito chats keep the conversation out of memory and chat history, which suits short-lived sensitive drafting. They don't override your organisation's retention configuration or admin visibility, so the content still has to be appropriate for the company seat.
distractors: Asking the model to forget doesn't change what memory or history has stored.
A shared Project makes the material visible to every member: the opposite of what you need.
Company material on a personal account is a policy breach, whatever the plan's settings.

items.scenario: You're about to share a Kubernetes manifest with Claude to debug a crash loop. It references a Secret by name, and an env block holds a database URL with an embedded password.
items.question: What do you do before pasting?
options: Nothing; manifests are internal material, so they're fine on a company seat
Replace the password with a placeholder, grep to confirm, keep the rest
Base64-encode the password so it isn't readable in the pasted manifest
Delete the whole env block, including the variable names, before pasting
items.explanation: Credentials are never-paste, whatever the plan. Redact the value and keep the structure Claude needs for debugging; the Secret's name is not the secret.
distractors: The manifest is internal, but the embedded credential is restricted. Classification follows the most sensitive item.
Base64 is encoding, not encryption. It's trivially reversible.
Over-redaction. Variable names are often key to diagnosing a crash loop.

items.scenario: A client asks how long data your team processes with Claude for them is retained. A colleague quotes a retention figure from a public blog post.
items.question: What governs the answer you give?
options: The figure in the blog post, since it describes the vendor's standard policy
Your org's contract terms and admin-set retention, confirmed with them
Whatever Claude says when you ask it about its own data retention
The consumer privacy policy, because it applies to every Claude plan
items.explanation: Retention on commercial plans is set by your organisation's agreement and its admins' configuration, and your contract overrides general guidance. Confirm with whoever owns those settings before telling a client anything.
distractors: General guidance doesn't reflect your organisation's own terms and settings.
The model doesn't know your organisation's configuration.
Consumer terms don't govern commercial plans, which have their own agreements.

items.scenario: You paste 340 expense lines as text and ask Claude for the total, which will go on a client invoice.
items.question: How should you get a total you can rely on?
options: Use Claude's total; adding up numbers is simple for a capable model
Have the sum computed by a tool (code or a spreadsheet) and spot-check it
Ask for the total twice in separate chats and use it if both agree
Re-run the request at Max effort so the model checks its own addition
items.explanation: Exact arithmetic without a tool is a known weak spot: models predict digits rather than calculate. Route the calculation through code execution or a spreadsheet and check the result before it reaches a client.
distractors: Long sums are exactly where unaided arithmetic slips.
Two runs can agree and still both be wrong; consistency isn't correctness.
More thinking reduces but doesn't remove arithmetic error; a tool computes exactly.

items.scenario: Yesterday, in another chat, you and Claude agreed naming conventions for a new service. Today, in a fresh chat on the same seat, Claude ignores them.
items.question: What explains this, and what's the durable fix?
options: A model update overnight changed its behaviour; pin yesterday's model
Chats share no state; put the conventions in a Project or instructions
Yesterday's chat expired; ask Claude to reload your earlier session
Claude disagrees with the conventions; repeat them more forcefully
items.explanation: Each chat starts fresh: the only carry-over is memory (if enabled) and Projects. Anything you want applied every time belongs in persistent instructions, not in a past conversation.
distractors: Nothing here points to a model change; a new chat simply doesn't contain yesterday's agreement.
There is no session to reload into a new chat; past chats aren't read automatically.
It isn't disagreeing; it never saw the conventions in this chat.

items.scenario: Claude's draft design rationale cites 'RFC 9876 §4.2' and a 2023 paper with three named authors to justify a retry strategy.
items.question: What should you do before circulating it?
options: Keep them; specific section numbers show the citations are genuine
Look up each reference and confirm it exists and says what is claimed
Ask Claude to confirm that both references are real before you send it
Remove the citations so readers don't question the design reasoning
items.explanation: Invented references are a known failure mode, and specific-looking details make them more convincing, not more real. Check each one at the source.
distractors: Precision is not evidence; fabricated references are often very specific.
The model can confirm its own fabrication; self-checking isn't independent.
Hiding the citations hides the problem; if the support is invented, the reasoning needs re-checking.

items.scenario: A prompt reads: 'Write something about the outage for the team.' The output is generic and too long. The update will be pasted by the support team to customers.
items.question: Which rewrite fixes the most defects?
options: 'Write a short, professional outage summary for the team. Be clear, no jargon.'
'You are a senior SRE and expert communicator. Write about today's outage.'
'Support will paste this to customers: 120 words on impact, status, next update.'
'Write about the outage. Don't be generic. Don't be long. Don't use jargon.'
items.explanation: It supplies the audience, the reason (customers will read it), the length, and the required content (impact, status, next update), fixing the vague task, missing context, format and audience together.
distractors: 'Short' and 'professional' are vague, and it still never says who reads it or what it must contain.
A role alone leaves the task, content, audience and length undefined.
Prohibitions without positive specification leave Claude guessing what you want.

items.scenario: A script will parse Claude's ticket-triage output and write each result into your ticketing system.
items.question: How should the prompt specify the output?
options: A readable markdown table, with one row per ticket and a notes column
Short prose for each ticket so the reasoning is preserved in the record
Exact JSON-like fields per ticket (id, severity, team), shown by example
Bullet points per ticket, letting Claude choose the clearest wording
items.explanation: Choose the format for the downstream use. A program needs fixed field names and values it can parse, so specify them and show an example that mirrors the output you want.
distractors: Tables suit people; free-text columns and formatting variations break parsers.
Prose has no fixed structure for a script to extract.
Free wording produces inconsistent structure that a parser can't rely on.

items.scenario: You want Claude to explain a Kafka consumer-lag alert. The explanation is for a new on-call engineer from the frontend team who has never touched the data platform.
items.question: Which addition most improves the explanation?
options: 'You are a world-class Kafka expert with 20 years of experience.'
'Reader: a frontend engineer new to Kafka, on call; define each term.'
'Explain it thoroughly, covering every possible cause of consumer lag.'
'Keep it simple and avoid all technical terms so anyone can follow it.'
items.explanation: Naming the reader and their background sets depth, vocabulary and what to explain; a role alone doesn't.
distractors: A role sets the voice of the writer, not the needs of the reader.
Exhaustiveness buries an on-call engineer who needs the likely causes and first actions.
Avoiding all terms leaves them unable to read the dashboards and runbook that use them.

items.scenario: You're asking Claude to estimate effort for migrating a legacy service, but team size, test coverage and the target platform are still uncertain.
items.question: Which addition to the prompt most improves the usefulness of the answer?
options: 'Be as accurate as you possibly can, since leadership will use this.'
'List the assumptions you made and the open questions that would change it.'
'Answer with a single number of engineer-weeks, with no qualifications.'
'Assume a typical team and typical coverage, and don't mention gaps.'
items.explanation: Asking for assumptions and open questions alongside the answer makes the gaps visible and reviewable instead of silently filled with guesses.
distractors: An instruction to be accurate adds no information.
A bare number hides the uncertainty you most need to see.
That instructs the model to hide the guesses you need to review.

items.scenario: You ask Claude to turn a messy restore procedure into a runbook. Each attempt reorders steps and sometimes drops 'verify the backup checksum', which must happen before the restore.
items.question: What change to the prompt fixes this most directly?
options: Add 'IMPORTANT: DO NOT SKIP ANY STEP!!!' at the very top of the prompt
Give the required steps as a numbered list and say the order is fixed
Ask for a shorter runbook so there are fewer steps to keep in order
Raise the effort level so the model reasons harder about the order
items.explanation: Numbered steps with a stated order make the sequence explicit and checkable. Saying why the checksum step comes first helps further.
distractors: Shouting adds emphasis but no structure, and can over-trigger caution elsewhere.
Shortening invites dropping exactly the step you need.
The problem is an unspecified sequence, not reasoning depth.

items.scenario: Claude drafted your weekly client status email from stand-up notes. It reads: 'The reporting export will ship next sprint.' Internally this was only a stretch goal.
items.question: Which part of sending discipline catches this?
options: Checking that the tone fits a client executive before sending
Checking every commitment against what was actually agreed
Checking the names and roles of everyone on the recipient list
Checking that every date and number matches the stand-up notes
items.explanation: Read before send means checking every name, number and commitment. Drafting turns tentative internal language into confident statements, so anything that reads as a promise must have been agreed by someone with authority.
distractors: Tone can be perfect while the content makes an unauthorised promise.
Names matter, but this sentence contains no name; the error is a promise.
There's no number or date here to mismatch; 'next sprint' is a commitment problem.

items.scenario: A colleague whose first language isn't English asks Claude to proofread a client proposal. Claude returns a fully rewritten version that reads well but has changed two scope statements.
items.question: What should they have asked for?
options: A full rewrite in fluent business English, then a quick skim to send
Corrections only, each shown with the original and a short reason
A rewrite in their first language, then a machine translation back
A shorter version, since concise text has fewer errors to proofread
items.explanation: Proofreading is a line edit: correct and explain each change so the author can accept selectively and keep the meaning. Anything contractual still gets a fluent human check.
distractors: A rewrite is exactly how the scope statements changed; skimming won't catch it.
Round-trip translation adds two chances for meaning drift.
Cutting changes content, which is the opposite of proofreading.

items.scenario: A 40-page platform design uses 'tenant', 'customer' and 'account' interchangeably, and two sections give different p95 latency targets.
items.question: Which Claude pass addresses this best?
options: Rewrite the whole document in one pass for clarity and flow
Check it against a glossary and list every conflicting figure
Shorten every section by a third so there's less to disagree
Read it as an executive and summarise the main design points
items.explanation: A consistency pass with an enforced glossary returns violations (location, used term, correct term) and conflicting numbers for you to resolve; you keep control of which value is right.
distractors: A full rewrite may pick one term and silently choose a latency figure without telling you.
Cutting doesn't resolve contradictions and may remove needed detail.
A summary hides inconsistencies rather than surfacing them.

items.scenario: Your client-facing incident report, drafted with Claude, is ready to send. Company policy requires a verification note on client-facing text.
items.question: What should the note record?
options: That Claude drafted the report, with the model name and the date
What was checked, how, and by whom, with a named person signing off
Claude's own confidence rating for each section of the report
A list of the prompts used, so the client can reproduce the draft
items.explanation: A verification note is evidence of human checking: what was checked, how, and by whom, with a named owner. (The full process is M8.2 at Practitioner.)
distractors: Disclosure of AI use may be required elsewhere, but it says nothing about whether the content is correct.
Model self-confidence isn't verification.
Prompts show how it was made, not that it was checked.

items.scenario: Through the Gmail connector you ask Claude to reply to a client who wants the go-live moved forward a week. Your team hasn't decided yet.
items.question: What is the right way to handle the reply?
options: Let Claude send a reply agreeing to the date, to keep the client happy
Have Claude draft a holding reply, then review and send it yourself
Let Claude reply that it's impossible, since nothing has been agreed
Skip a reply until the team decides, however long that ends up taking
items.explanation: Claude drafts, you send. A holding reply acknowledges the request without committing, and you check the wording before anything goes out; Workspace write actions also ask for approval by default.
distractors: Commits the team to a date nobody agreed.
Also a commitment the team hasn't made, in the other direction.
Silence with a client is its own communication failure; a holding reply is the standard move.

items.scenario: You can see your org's Confluence connector and its search tool, but Claude reports that the 'update_page' tool is unavailable when you ask it to fix a typo on a page.
items.question: What is the most likely reason?
options: The connector is broken and should be removed and added again
An admin enabled the connector but disabled its write tools
Claude refuses to edit pages, so the typo must be fixed by hand
Your Confluence account has lost access to that page's space
items.explanation: Admins control connectors per connector and per tool, for example enabling read tools while disabling writes. Ask the admin if the write is genuinely needed.
distractors: Search works, so the connector is fine; reinstalling won't restore a tool an admin disabled.
It isn't a model refusal; the tool isn't exposed to the session.
A permission problem would affect the page, not make the tool itself unavailable.

items.scenario: A developer wants Claude to query your internal deployment API, which has no connector. They plan to paste a personal access token into the chat and let Claude 'figure out the calls'.
items.question: What's the right path?
options: Paste the token, but revoke it as soon as the chat session ends
Ask the admins for an approved custom connector for that API
Share a read-only token instead, since it can't change anything
Let Claude in Chrome sign in to the API console with your account
items.explanation: Internal systems are reached through custom connectors (remote MCP servers) added by whoever your plan allows, typically admins on Team and Enterprise. Tokens never go into a prompt.
distractors: The token is already exposed once pasted; revoking later doesn't undo that.
Read-only tokens are still credentials, and reads can expose sensitive data.
Puts a browser agent in your signed-in session against an API console: wide blast radius, not auditable.

items.scenario: Claude's answer says 'I checked all three team calendars and found no conflicts.' The tool-call trail shows a single list_events call against your own calendar.
items.question: What do you conclude?
options: The summary is right; the tool probably queried all three in one call
The trail is the record; only your calendar was checked, so re-scope
The connector logs incompletely, so trust the summary over the trail
Nothing; calendar checks are low risk, so the detail doesn't matter
items.explanation: Reading the tool calls is what makes connector use auditable. The trail shows what Claude actually looked at; the summary overstated it. Re-run with the three calendars named explicitly.
distractors: The call's arguments show which calendar was queried; don't assume beyond them.
The trail is the evidence; summaries are where overstatement happens.
A missed conflict means a wrong decision, whatever the risk level of the call.

items.scenario: You asked Claude to email the vendor's account manager a meeting summary. The approval prompt shows send_email to an address at a different domain, with the full internal notes attached.
items.question: What do you do?
options: Approve; you asked for an email, and Claude chose the right recipient
Deny, check the recipient and content, and look for an injection
Approve, then email the vendor afterwards to delete the message
Approve, since approval prompts are a formality for routine mail
items.explanation: The approval prompt is the control only if you read it: recipient, target and content. A wrong domain plus over-sharing is a red flag for a mistake or an injected instruction.
distractors: You asked for a specific recipient; a different domain needs explaining before anything is sent.
A sent email can't be recalled; asking the recipient to delete it is not a control.
Treating approvals as a formality is exactly how exfiltration gets through.

items.scenario: You've finished a first Claude Code session in a service repo. Tomorrow's sessions should already know how to build, test and lint it, and which directories are off-limits.
items.question: What's the best way to capture this?
options: Repeat the build and test commands at the start of every new session
Run /init, then edit the CLAUDE.md it drafts and commit it to the repo
Use /compact at the end of today so the summary carries to tomorrow
Tell Claude to remember the commands; today's chat carries over
items.explanation: CLAUDE.md is loaded at the start of every session. /init drafts one from the repo; you correct it, keep it short and commit it so the whole team shares it.
distractors: Works, but relies on memory and drifts between people.
Compaction summarises the current session; a new session doesn't start from it.
A new session doesn't load yesterday's conversation; CLAUDE.md is loaded every time and is shared via Git.

items.scenario: You're making many small documentation fixes across a repo you know well, on a branch. You'll review the whole diff at the end, but want to approve any shell command first.
items.question: Which permission mode fits?
options: default (Manual)
acceptEdits
plan
bypassPermissions
items.explanation: acceptEdits applies file edits (and simple filesystem commands) in the working directory without asking, while other shell commands still ask. You review the edits afterwards with git diff.
distractors: Works, but prompts for every edit, which is the friction you've decided you don't need here.
Plan mode doesn't edit your files at all.
Removes the command approvals you want to keep, and belongs only in a sandbox or CI.

items.scenario: After installing Claude Code, `claude` starts but login fails and you suspect an older copy installed via npm is also on your PATH.
items.question: What is the best first step?
options: Reinstall with every method available until one of them works
Run the doctor health check and follow the fixes it reports
Switch to bypassPermissions so login isn't blocked by prompts
Ask in chat which install method is correct for your machine
items.explanation: The doctor check (`claude doctor` in the shell, /doctor in a session) reports install health, conflicting installations, auth and settings problems with suggested fixes.
distractors: Stacking installs makes the conflicting-installation problem worse.
Permission modes govern tool use in a session, not installation or login.
A chat answer can't see your PATH or installs; the health check can.

items.scenario: Claude's last turn refactored four files the wrong way. It ran no shell commands, and you haven't committed since the turn began.
items.question: What's the cleanest way to undo it?
options: /clear, which discards the session along with its file edits
/rewind to the prompt before that turn and restore the code
git reset --hard HEAD~1 to drop the most recent commit
/compact, then ask Claude to undo its refactor by hand
items.explanation: Checkpoints capture Claude's file edits at each prompt, so /rewind can restore the code to before that turn. Git (git restore) would also work for uncommitted changes.
distractors: /clear resets the conversation context; it doesn't touch files on disk.
Discards the uncommitted refactor only by also destroying your last real commit, which predates it.
Compaction summarises context; asking for a manual undo is slower and error-prone when a checkpoint exists.

items.scenario: A teammate says Claude Code 'can only touch files in the repo folder', so working in a repo next to their cloud credentials and SSH keys is harmless.
items.question: Which statement is accurate?
options: Correct; by default Claude Code is confined to the folder where it starts
Wrong; approved shell commands run as you and can reach those files
Correct, unless they also connect an MCP server to the session
Wrong, but only when running in bypassPermissions mode on Linux
items.explanation: By default Claude Code runs commands with your user's access: files beyond the repo, environment variables, the network and your Git credentials. Permission prompts, deny rules and (if you enable it) sandboxing are what bound it, which is why you never start with the widest permission.
distractors: File tools are scoped to the working directory, but approved shell commands run with your full user access.
MCP adds more reach, but shell commands can already touch files outside the repo.
Any mode that runs a command you approved can reach them; bypass only removes the prompts.
